 US apparel body urges annual minimum wage review in Bangladesh 
 In a letter to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, AAFA says regular adjustments would protect workers' purchasing power, ease recurring wage tensions and make increases more predictable for employers. 
 TBS Report 
 19 November, 2026, 11:25 pm 
 Last modified: 19 November, 2026, 11:34 pm 
 Photo: Collected "> 
 Photo: Collected 
 The American Apparel and Footwear Association (AAFA) has urged the Bangladesh government to introduce an annual minimum wage review mechanism for the readymade garment (RMG) sector, warning that prolonged gaps between revisions erode workers' purchasing power and fuel recurring labour unrest. 
 In a letter dated 15 November to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, AAFA President and CEO Stephen Lamar said the garment-sector minimum wage had not been adjusted since 2023, despite a significant rise in inflation and higher energy costs that have increased pressure on households.
 "We continue to recommend the government of Bangladesh adopt an annual minimum wage review mechanism to prevent the erosion of workers' purchasing power, reduce recurrent tensions in the wage-setting process, and promote more gradual and predictable wage adjustments for both workers and employers," the letter said.
 Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel
 The association welcomed the government's formation of a Minimum Wage Board and its engagement with employers and labour representatives to address concerns behind the recent protests.
 It said the wage review offered an opportunity to establish a fair wage that would enable garment workers to support themselves and their families, while taking account of Bangladesh's economic realities and the long-term sustainability of the sector.
 AAFA called for an inclusive, transparent and evidence-based process involving all relevant stakeholders, including labour groups and trade unions.
 It also urged the government to ensure effective tripartite consultations in line with International Labour Organization (ILO) principles on wage-setting, with full respect for freedom of association and collective bargaining rights.
 The association said the revised minimum wage should be sufficient to cover workers' basic needs and provide some discretionary income, while taking inflationary pressures and the country's economic situation into account.
 The letter also called on the government to prevent violence, threats and intimidation against union members and ensure that workers and labour leaders face no retaliation for participating in the wage review.
 It specifically urged authorities to prevent violence against peaceful protesters and arrests of union leaders, saying such safeguards were necessary to build confidence in wage-setting institutions and strengthen social dialogue.
 AAFA also stressed the responsibility of international brands and retailers sourcing from Bangladesh, saying responsible purchasing practices and appropriate consideration of labour costs in pricing were essential to support better wages and working conditions.
 The association said its members were committed to responsible purchasing practices.
 AAFA represents more than 1,100 apparel, footwear and sewn-products brands, according to the letter. It said the US-Bangladesh partnership in the garment, footwear and travel goods industries had helped make Bangladesh the third-largest supplier of garments and a fast-growing supplier of footwear and travel goods to the United States and global markets.
 The letter comes amid continued labour unrest in Bangladesh's garment sector, where workers have been demanding an increase in the monthly minimum wage from Tk12,500 to Tk30,000, alongside the reinstatement of dismissed workers and an end to blacklisting.
 The government formed a six-member Minimum Wage Board on 1 November to review the sector's wage structure.
